data.title: Nevus of Ota / Ito / Hori — viva
data.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nevus of Ota / Ito / Hori** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. Write a short note on nevus of Ota (PYQ).**
- Dermal melanocytosis (oculodermal melanocytosis) with blue-grey to brown mottled patch in the distribution of the 1st and 2nd branches of the trigeminal nerve (forehead, temple, periorbital, malar), unilateral in ~90%; ipsilateral scleral (blue-grey) and ocular involvement in ~2/3
- Asian and Indian women more; onset at birth (50%) or around puberty (second peak); GNAQ/GNA11 mutations
- Mucosa (palate, nasal), tympanic membrane may be involved

**Q2. Tanino classification.**
- Type I mild (Ia orbital, Ib zygomatic), II moderate (V1+V2 area), III intensive (scalp, forehead, nose), IV bilateral

**Q3. Complications.**
- Glaucoma (ipsilateral — regular eye checks), uveal/ choroidal melanoma (especially in white patients), CNS melanoma (rare), sensorineural hearing loss; associated with Sturge–Weber/Klippel–Trenaunay (phakomatosis pigmentovascularis)

**Q4. What is nevus of Ito and Hori's naevus?**
- Nevus of Ito: same dermal melanocytosis in the distribution of posterior supraclavicular and lateral cutaneous brachial nerves (shoulder, supraclavicular, scapula, upper arm)
- Hori's naevus (acquired bilateral naevus of Ota-like macules — ABNOM): acquired in middle-aged Asian women, bilateral blue-brown speckled macules on malar areas, forehead, eyelids; no ocular/mucosal involvement; often misdiagnosed as melasma

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Elongated, dendritic, pigmented melanocytes scattered among collagen bundles in the upper and mid dermis (dermal melanocytes) — superficial, deep or diffuse types; epidermis normal

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Melasma (bilateral brown, no blue-grey or eye involvement), Mongolian spot (sacral, fades), blue naevus, lichen planus pigmentosus, drug pigmentation (minocycline), PIH, port-wine stain (early), ecchymosis

**Q7. Management.**
- Q-switched lasers (Nd:YAG 1064 nm — preferred in dark skin, alexandrite 755 nm, ruby 694 nm) or picosecond lasers — multiple sessions (5–10) 2–3 months apart; excellent response (selective photothermolysis of dermal melanin); risk of PIH/hypopigmentation, recurrence
- Ophthalmology review (glaucoma, melanoma) at baseline and periodically; camouflage

**Q8. Describe the clinical features of nevus of Ota.**
- Unilateral (90%) blue-grey/ brown speckled macular pigmentation in V1–V2 trigeminal distribution (forehead, temple, periorbital, malar, nose), with scleral/ conjunctival pigmentation in ~2/3; bimodal onset — infancy and puberty; women and Asians (incl. Indians) more

**Q9. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Arrested migration of neural-crest melanocytes in the dermis; GNAQ/GNA11 mutations; hormonal influence (appears/ darkens at puberty, pregnancy)

**Q10. Hori's naevus (ABNOM) vs melasma.**
- Hori's: bilateral speckled blue-brown/ grey macules on malar region, temples, eyelids, nasal ala in Asian women 20–40 y, no ocular involvement; dermal melanocytosis on histology — Q-switched lasers effective
- Melasma: brown confluent symmetrical patches with epidermal ± dermal pigment, worse with sun; different treatment (lasers worsen)

**Q11. What is Mongolian spot vs nevus of Ota?**
- Mongolian (dermal melanocytosis) spot: blue-grey patch over lumbosacral region in Asian/ African neonates, fades by childhood; extensive/ persistent spots associated with lysosomal storage disorders (GM1 gangliosidosis, Hurler) and phacomatosis pigmentovascularis

**Q12. Malignant transformation risk.**
- Rare melanoma of skin, orbit, uveal tract, leptomeninges (CNS) — especially with ocular involvement; annual eye and skin examination

**Q13. Q-switched laser protocol tips.**
- Q-switched Nd:YAG 1064 nm (dark skin), alexandrite 755 nm, ruby 694 nm; 4–10 sessions at 2–3 monthly intervals; endpoint — immediate whitening; side effects — transient PIH, hypopigmentation, recurrence (rare); picosecond lasers fewer sessions

**Q14. What lasers are used and why?**
- Q-switched (nanosecond) ruby 694 nm, alexandrite 755 nm and Nd:YAG 1064 nm (best for dark skin) and picosecond lasers — selective photothermolysis of dermal melanin; multiple sessions every 2–3 months; complications: hyper/hypopigmentation, textural change; excellent response, earlier treatment in childhood needs fewer sessions

**Q15. Why examine the eyes?**
- Ocular melanocytosis (sclera, conjunctiva, iris) in ~2/3; risk of glaucoma (~10%) and uveal/ choroidal melanoma — yearly ophthalmological follow-up with intraocular pressure measurement

## Quick spotter facts
- Unilateral blue-grey patch on V1/V2 with scleral pigmentation — nevus of Ota
- Q-switched Nd:YAG laser
- Bilateral acquired malar blue-brown macules — Hori's naevus

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Dermal melanocytoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
